name: Colin Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Marsh End, which is the Brennan family's farm on the flat land by the river. It's two hundred hectares of potatoes, sugar beet and wheat, and a herd of ninety suckler cows, which means beef cows that raise their own calves. I'm one of two workers, with the son, Liam, who'll take it over one day. Spring I'm planting, summer it's spraying and silage, autumn is potato and beet lifting, which is fourteen-hour days on the harvester, and winter is mostly the cattle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lifting season, strangely, because you can see what you've done at the end of the day, a full shed. What wears me out is that the pay doesn't move. I've been there six years and I'm about where I started. My partner Nina is in her second year training as a nurse, so it's mostly my wage for now, and we've got about three weeks saved. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to settle arguments or check a spray rate when the label's worn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was useful for a few things and that's it. I'd probably joke at the pub that the robot uprising got cancelled. I don't post much online, maybe a football thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay as they are, and for me that's mostly fine, apart from the pay. Liam's going to take over the farm and he'll keep me on. The thing I'm waiting for isn't a robot, it's Nina qualifying so we've got two proper wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep using the chat thing for the odd spray rate. I'd ask Liam's dad for a raise again in the spring, maybe with a bit more push this time. We'd keep saving a bit for a house deposit once Nina's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much more push would you give the raise this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what the contractor down the road pays for harvester drivers, which is about fifteen percent more. I wouldn't threaten to leave, because I don't really want to. But I'd want him to know I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When Nina qualifies, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look for a house in the village, something small. We've been saying that for two years. It'd be nice to stop renting from Liam's uncle.

S0.say: Fair enough, it was useful for a few things and that's it. He'd joke at the pub that the robot uprising got cancelled.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, which suits him apart from the low pay. What he's really waiting for is his partner qualifying as a nurse so they have two wages.
S0.do: Keeps working and using the AI chat tool occasionally for spray rates. Asks for a raise in spring, citing what the local contractor pays. Keeps saving for a house deposit.
S0.quote: The thing I'm waiting for isn't a robot, it's Nina qualifying so we've got two proper wages.
S0.fieldNote: Colin's horizon is his partner's nursing qualification and a house in the village, not technology. He's steady and quietly ambitious about pay, knowing his market rate without threatening to leave. He trusts the farmer's son to keep him on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks changing. Yeah, the harvester would be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be sensible about it and learn what we need. I wouldn't be for or against it, just practical. At the pub I'd probably argue with Dev, who thinks it's all a scam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the self-driving tractors would come to farms like Marsh End within a few years, and the harvester would follow. Liam's keen on that kind of thing. He'd keep me on, I think, but as the bloke who watches the screen, and he'd say that's why he can't pay me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger farms do for a year or so, then learn the systems once they'd proved themselves. I'd use the chat tool more, maybe to understand the tractor software. I'd go to the dealer's open day when they show the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it niggles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Liam would use the robots as a reason not to pay you more. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From his side, probably. From mine, no. If I'm running two machines instead of driving one, I'm doing more, not less. But I can see how the conversation would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nina say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say at least nurses aren't going anywhere. She might be right, she might not. She'd tell me to start learning now and not wait, because that's her, and I'm more of a wait-and-see bloke.

S1.say: It's coming, so let's be sensible and learn what we need. He'd stay neither for nor against, just practical.
S1.think: Self-driving tractors and harvesters would reach the farm soon. He'd likely be kept on to watch the screens but with even less bargaining power for a raise.
S1.do: Watches what bigger farms do for about a year, then learns the systems once proven. Uses the chat tool more to understand tractor software. Goes to the dealer's open day.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a niggle rather than fear.
S1.quote: He'd keep me on, I think, but as the bloke who watches the screen, and he'd say that's why he can't pay me more.
S1.fieldNote: Colin expects to keep his job but lose bargaining power, which is a sharp and specific worry. He contrasts himself with his partner, who would act sooner. His plan is to follow once others have proved the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Bloody hell. That's two lifting seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to get a grip, quickly. Someone has to make sure people still have money coming in, because there's no way the farms will. I'd say it calmly enough, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be gone. If a robot can drive the harvester and handle the cattle, Liam doesn't need me, and he'd tell me that kindly. Nina wouldn't even have qualified yet. We'd go from one wage to none, with three weeks in the bank and a deposit we never saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money towards the house and keep it as a cushion instead. We'd cut back, the car insurance, the takeaways, the phone contracts. I'd look for anything else nearby, delivery driving or warehouse work, while there still is some, and we'd talk to Nina's parents about help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake on that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say finish the course, whatever happens. If anyone's going to have a job, it's someone who looks after people. I'd do the rest, whatever it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're a wait-and-see person. Does that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There's nothing to wait for in two years. I'd have to move before it's proven, which isn't how I like to do things, but that's the situation.

S2.say: The government needs to get a grip quickly and keep money coming in for people. He'd say it calmly but mean it.
S2.think: He'd likely be let go before his partner qualifies, leaving them with no wages and three weeks of savings. The house deposit would never happen.
S2.do: Stops saving for a house and keeps the money as a cushion. Cuts car insurance, takeaways and phone contracts. Looks for delivery or warehouse work and asks his partner's parents for help.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep. Protective of his partner's course.
S2.quote: We'd go from one wage to none, with three weeks in the bank and a deposit we never saved.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's first instinct is to protect his partner's nursing course at all costs. He knows his wait-and-see habit fails here and says so plainly. The house plan dies first, which shows how much it meant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right, so Nina's qualified and working by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's do it properly. Farms and colleges should be training people now. I'd say that at the farmers' discussion group, which I go to sometimes with Liam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes a lot for us because Nina would have a proper wage by then. I'd still lose the harvester job, but we wouldn't be on nothing. Five years means she carries us for a bit, and I'd have to get used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the house deposit on hold and save it as a cushion, maybe eighty a month. Once Nina's working, I'd look at retraining, maybe as a heavy goods driver or a technician, but I'd wait a year or two to see which jobs held up. I'd keep working at Marsh End as long as Liam needed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A clear worry, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about Nina carrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit funny. It's not that I mind her earning more. It's that I've always been the one with the steady job and she's been the student, and that would flip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina's qualification, mainly. In two years we're on nothing. In five we're on one wage, and that's survivable, with time for me to pick something else.

S3.say: There's time to get ready, so farms and colleges should start training people now. He'd raise it at the farmers' discussion group.
S3.think: By then his partner would be qualified and working, so he'd lose his job but they'd still have one wage. He'd have to get used to being carried for a while.
S3.do: Saves about eighty a month as a cushion instead of a house deposit. Considers retraining as a heavy goods driver or technician after his partner starts work, waiting to see which jobs hold up. Stays on the farm as long as possible.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, with some discomfort about the roles flipping.
S3.quote: Five years means she carries us for a bit, and I'd have to get used to that.
S3.fieldNote: The warning time matters to Colin mostly because of his partner's qualification date. He's open about feeling odd if she becomes the main earner. He still prefers to wait before picking a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Liam's dad would be retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan for, and I'd plan. I'd want the government to fund retraining for people my age, not just kids. I'd be fairly upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could see which jobs survive and move into one in good time. Nina would be settled as a nurse, we'd maybe have a house by then. I'd rather be the bloke fixing the robot harvester than the bloke it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving for the house, actually, because there'd be time. In three or four years, once it was clear which machines farms were buying, I'd do a course to service them, the dealer runs an apprenticeship. I'd use the chat tool more as I went along, once I'd seen what it was good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Marsh End through all that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for most of it. Liam's alright, and I'd like to be the one who sets up his machines before I move on. If I'm going to be replaced, I'd at least like to install the thing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might mean we start one. With two years, no chance. With ten, I'd think we'd have a house and two jobs of some sort, so yes, maybe.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to plan, and he'd plan. The government should fund retraining for people his age, not just young people.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to see which jobs survive and move into one in time. He'd rather fix the robot harvester than be replaced by it.
S4.do: Keeps saving for a house. Takes a dealer apprenticeship to service farm machines in three or four years, once it's clear what farms are buying. Uses the chat tool more as he goes.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not.
S4.quote: If I'm going to be replaced, I'd at least like to install the thing myself.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Colin's house plans come back and he even talks about a family. His wish to install his own replacement is a dry, telling line. He still waits for the market to show its hand before choosing a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Nina wouldn't have qualified and we'd have nothing coming in. What would help is some kind of wage for people who lose their jobs before they've had time to prepare, and help for her to finish her course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the landlord. We rent from Liam's uncle, and if Marsh End goes over to robots, I'm not sure we'd stay welcome in the cottage either. Everything round here is tied together.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the bloke fixing the robot harvester than the bloke it replaced.
portrait: Colin Alvarez is a 27-year-old worker on a 200-hectare potato, beet and beef farm, where he drives the harvester and expects the farmer's son to keep him on. His partner Nina is training as a nurse, so they live mostly on his low wage with about three weeks of savings. Pragmatic and steady, he uses AI tools now and then and prefers to wait until new kit is proven. He's calm at a plateau, uneasy at steady change because he'd lose bargaining power, and alarmed at AGI in two years when they'd have no wage. With more warning, his partner's qualification becomes the turning point, and with ten years he plans to service the machines and revives hopes of a house and family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his partner wouldn't yet be qualified and they'd have no income.
whatWouldHelp: A wage for people who lose jobs before they can prepare, and help so his partner can finish her nursing course.
